papers.title: Data Driven Modeling of a Magnetic Newton's Cradle using the Optimization of a Discrete Loss
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of a magnetic Newton's cradle (MNC) using experiments, simulations through forward and inverse data driven models. In the MNC magnetic forces replace the instantaneous elastic collisions of the classical design. We compare point-dipole and finite-current-loop interaction models, identifying their parameters from direct measurements as well as through pendulum trajectories using the method of Optimizing a Discrete Loss (ODIL). For a synthetic three-pendulum twin, ODIL reproduces discretized trajectories to round-off accuracy and infers accurately magnet strength and damping from sparse data even when only one pendulum is observed. Model comparison shows that the point-dipole model compensates for near-field errors by underestimating the magnetic moment and produces structured residuals at each momentum transfer. The current-loop model removes this bias and, on full-precision recordings, also recovers the magnet radius. The continuous magnetic coupling reproduces the classical cradle's key behavior while enabling richer dynamics, including $N$ normal modes and a static repulsion offset. These results demonstrate that ODIL can infer physical parameters, and quantify model-form errors from sparse, noisy observations. Ultimately, this work establishes the magnetic Newton's cradle not merely as a physical curiosity, but as a rigorously quantifiable testbed for computational inverse modeling.

papers.title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
papers.abstract: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

papers.title: Walk on Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable and Composable Transport Medium Prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE Solvers
papers.abstract: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials. We introduce Walk on Multiscale Media (WoMM), which compiles fine-scale transport into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs. A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions retaining fine-scale material effects. Each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, enabling incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion. Integrated with conventional Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous--discrete solver, these prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem.

papers.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
papers.abstract: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

papers.title: Dual Area-Volume-of-Fluid (DAVOF): co-advecting volume and face-area fractions for a closed-form, cell-local interface normal and position on unstructured meshes
papers.abstract: Geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) on unstructured polyhedral meshes reconstructs the interface orientation from the volume fractions of a stencil of neighbours; on irregular cells and in the presence of wisps it degrades, and the curvature built on it drives the parasitic currents of capillary flows. We transport, consistently to the volume fraction of every cell, the wetted fraction of every face area. From the area and volume fractions, closed-form equations recover the interface normal and position of a cell, for the first time in VOF: the normal from one sum over the cell's own faces, the divergence theorem on the liquid sub-volume, and the plane's position from a second, without neighbours or iteration. Both identities are exact for a plane on hexahedral, perturbed and polyhedral cells. On a sphere and an ellipsoid the normal has the order of the face fractions, the position is second order for every state and mesh, and a quadric through one ring of recovered normals gives a converging curvature where the reference models show none. Transported with the plane clipping, the ring normal, the same identity on the union of the cell's ring, stabilises the state and carries a sphere over 3.3 diameters bounded and conservative, first order in the face fractions as the clipping law predicts, at plicRDF's position and shape errors. A preliminary transport implementation with one paraboloid per cell, its frame from the normal, its curvature tensor from the ring and its position from the volume fraction, carries the sphere bounded and conservative over the resolution ladder with face fractions of order 2.8 per period with the exact normal and 2.1 with the ring quadric's normal over N = 32 to 128. The loop has the order of the normal it is fed; a transported normal of second order is the research goal. This document is the basis on which the further development of the method is documented.

papers.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

papers.title: Hidden Phase Transition in Single-Polymer Stretching under Elongational Flow
papers.abstract: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model reproduces both transitions and shows that they are phase transitions in the long-chain limit. Single-molecule DNA experiments provide qualitative support for the dynamical transition through the predicted reversal of the folding response.

papers.title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
papers.abstract: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

papers.title: Quantum-inspired space-time PDE solver and dynamic mode decomposition
papers.abstract: The numerical solution of time-dependent PDEs posed over the combined space-time domain, instead of treating time sequentially, leads to space-time methods. Treating time as another spatial dimension allows parallelization across time and simultaneous adaptivity in spatial and temporal discretizations. However, space-time formulations suffer from the curse of dimensionality due to the (d+1)-dimensional domain. Time-series forecasting methods, such as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), also suffer the same scaling for storing and processing measurement data. In this work, we investigate whether quantum-inspired tensor network methods can mitigate this curse for both solving PDEs and data-driven modeling. We formulate a space-time matrix product state (MPS) encoding to represent either the space-time solution or time-series data. Using this representation, we develop a unified framework that combines an MPS space-time PDE solver with an MPS-DMD algorithm. We benchmark our MPS space-time solver for linear and nonlinear PDEs in both (1+1) and (2+1) dimensions, including non-diffusive regimes such as shockwave formation and Allen-Cahn phase separation. We observe that the MPS ansatz efficiently captures the spatio-temporal correlations of the solutions, with a 99% reduction in parameters with respect to the grid size. We demonstrate the MPS-DMD algorithm in two cases. First, the MPS space-time solver generates the MPS encoding of the time-series data. We then apply MPS-DMD directly to predict the dynamics without solving PDEs. Second, for the general case where data is available as dense arrays, MPS-DMD needs an intermediate compression step. We implement a streaming-like compression algorithm and observe a 97% reduction in memory, with MPS-DMD predictions matching those of exact DMD.

papers.title: Point-Group Equivariant Neural Networks for Local Dynamics in Lattice Systems
papers.abstract: We develop point-group equivariant neural networks for learning local mappings used in dynamical simulations of lattice systems. The same network acts on a finite neighborhood around each site, respecting lattice translations through shared parameters. The local configuration is decomposed into features that transform according to irreducible representations of the point group, and hidden features retain this organization throughout the network. Equivariant linear maps and symmetry-allowed tensor products then learn nonlinear spatial correlations while preserving the required transformation laws. This approach avoids constructing a fixed set of hand-crafted invariant descriptors, whose selection requires choices about which local correlations to retain. It also allows the complexity of the learned mapping to grow without enlarging its spatial cutoff. We demonstrate the construction by learning the forces governing adiabatic dynamics in the square-lattice Holstein model. Comparisons with exact diagonalization test the accuracy of the predicted forces and the evolution of spatial correlations. Force evaluation scales linearly with system size, allowing the trained model to simulate charge-density-wave ordering on large lattices. These simulations reproduce anomalously slow coarsening of the charge-density-wave domains, illustrating the use of the learned local mapping for collective dynamics.

papers.title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
papers.abstract: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

papers.title: MoireKP: An Automated Workflow for Symmetry-Constrained Moir\'e Continuum Models
papers.abstract: First-principles Hamiltonians contain the electronic information needed to study moir\'e materials, but their size makes subsequent calculations costly. We present MoireKP, an automated workflow for constructing compact continuum models from localized-orbital ab initio Hamiltonians. The workflow constructs a valley-resolved truncated atomic-plane-wave (TAPW) Hamiltonian, selects a low-energy basis, and projects the crystal-symmetry operations into this basis. These representations determine the symmetry-allowed Hamiltonian terms, whose coefficients are obtained by projecting the low-energy effective Hamiltonian onto the corresponding operator basis. The model dimension, localized reference states, and harmonic cutoff can be selected automatically or specified by the user. This Hamiltonian-based construction retains wave-function information within the selected low-energy subspace. We apply the workflow to AA-stacked twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$, AB-stacked twisted bilayer ZrS$_2$, and A--AB twisted trilayer MoTe$_2$, covering K, M, and $\Gamma$ valleys. All models reproduce TAPW band energies within 3.0 meV in the target windows along high-symmetry $k$ paths.

papers.title: RAKI: High-Order Alternative Finite Differences for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) and black hole--neutron star mergers are among the most important multimessenger sources. Observations of these events could provide valuable insights into several unresolved phenomena, ranging from the efficiency of magnetic field amplification during and after mergers to the formation of magnetars and jets. Understanding these phenomena requires accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution, which remains a challenge for state-of-the-art general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In this work, we present \texttt{RAKI} (Relativistic Astrophysics Code Implementation of the Alternative Finite Difference Approach for GRMHD), the first GRMHD code to simulate BNS mergers using high-order alternative finite-difference methods with adaptive-order WENO (AFD-WENO-AO) reconstruction and a fully non-staggered, node-centred vector-potential formulation. The code achieves up to ninth-order convergence in smooth test problems while accurately capturing discontinuities. In magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) star tests, \texttt{RAKI} retains $99.2$ per cent of the initial maximum magnetic field strength over ${\sim}2$ ms, exhibiting an order of magnitude less magnetic field loss than a reference GRMHD code at the same resolution. In BNS merger simulations, fifth-order AFD-WENO-AO reconstruction yields approximately third-order convergence of the gravitational-wave phase in both magnetised and unmagnetised models. The discrete no-monopole constraint is preserved to machine precision without staggered grids, even during BNS mergers with moving refinement regions. These results establish \texttt{RAKI} as a high-order, non-staggered GRMHD framework for accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution in neutron star mergers and its implications for multimessenger astrophysics.

papers.title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

papers.title: Electric field control of anisotropic spin traffic between spin-filtering and magnon-scattering in a layered antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: Layered A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) semiconductors offer a unique platform for spintronic devices by combining robust magnetism with gate-tunable semiconducting properties. We present a dual-gate field-effect transistor based on CrSBr, a layered A-type AFM with pronounced transport anisotropy and complex spin dynamics. Our device provides independent control over carrier density and displacement field. Systematic transport measurements reveal that the displacement field, rather than doping, predominantly governs the sign and magnitude of magnetoresistance ratio (MRR). We identify the origins of both negative and positive MRR components and connect them to interlayer and intralayer spin-dependent transport mechanisms. We interpret these findings with ab initio calculations and an effective spin-circuit model that reproduces the anisotropic magnetotransport. Our results identify the displacement field as an efficient electrical control parameter of spin transport in CrSBr and suggest that multi-gate architectures could provide similar control in other layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

papers.title: Exploring Fractional Quantum Hall States with Deep Learning: From Abelian to Non-Abelian Phases
papers.abstract: Fractional quantum Hall systems host strongly correlated topological phases with potential applications in topological quantum computation, yet identifying their microscopic ground states remains challenging because competing phases are often nearly degenerate and Landau-level mixing is difficult to treat. Here, we introduce a symmetry-adapted neural-network wavefunction that describes Abelian and non-Abelian states while incorporating all Landau levels. The method accurately captures composite-fermion liquids and the emergence of Wigner crystallization at low filling. When the first Landau level is partially filled, finite-size overlaps and entanglement spectra provide evidence consistent with $\bar{2}^{k}1^{k+1}$-type parton phases at $\nu=4/3$ and $7/5$, while the $\nu=3/2$ state exhibits anti-Pfaffian-like entanglement structure. These results demonstrate that neural-network wavefunctions offer a flexible framework for studying competing topological orders in fractional quantum Hall systems.

papers.title: Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: The local field factor $G(q)$ of the HEG describes how exchange and correlation modify the response to a static perturbation, and enters dielectric screening, effective electron--electron interactions, and the xc kernel of TDDFT. Accurate zero-temperature data for $G(q)$, however, remain limited to metallic densities, $r_s\leq10$. In this work, we present diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density response function $\chi(q)$ and of $G(q)$ for $2\leq r_s\leq100$, and describe and discuss the methodological steps that enabled these calculations. We show how optimization of the perturbing potential in the trial wave function has an important effect, as a poor choice can reverse the sign of the response. A closed-form expression is provided for its optimal value, together with the density dependence of the linear-response window. We further show that backflow correlations leave $\chi(q)$ unchanged and that $G(q)$ depends only weakly on system size even at very low density, so that Slater--Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes suffice. Together, these results provide a practical guide for future QMC calculations of response properties of the electron gas and real materials. Our results agree with previous DMC data at metallic densities for $q>k_F$, and extend them below $k_F$. They also agree with diagrammatic QMC at $r_s=2$. At lower densities, our results show that $G(q)$ develops a nonmonotonic structure at intermediate-$q$, where the response approaches that of the noninteracting gas. Quantitative agreement is seen with finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo, suggesting that the previously reported finite-temperature structure is inherited from the ground state. Using a parametrization of $G(q)$ that reproduces our data throughout the liquid phase, we relate this structure to short-range order in the pair correlation function and the static structure factor.

papers.title: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.

papers.title: virasoro_blocks: Software for the 2d bootstrap
papers.abstract: We introduce virasoro_blocks, software that computes Virasoro conformal blocks at any central charge in a form suitable for the numerical bootstrap. At each finite order in the elliptic nome, Zamolodchikov's recursion gives the block as a positive prefactor times a rational function of the exchanged weight. However, its many Kac poles make it difficult to use in semidefinite programming approaches to the bootstrap. In this software we use optimal interpolation to reduce the number of poles while keeping high accuracy. The software works in arbitrary precision and handles singular central charges, including the minimal models and $c=1$. It also computes global blocks, $N=1$ superconformal blocks, torus characters, and torus one-point blocks. We illustrate it with two applications. Assuming only scalar Virasoro primaries, we compute bounds on the scalar gap that approach the window of Liouville solutions between $(c-1)/16$ and $(c-1)/12$. We also bound the average exchanged dimension in four-point functions of identical scalars at several central charges. These bounds have a rich structure, and many known 2d CFTs lie on or near their boundary.

papers.title: Ten-loop fixed-dimension renormalization-group functions of the three-dimensional O(N) model from distributed GPU-accelerated parametric integration
papers.abstract:
The renormalization-group functions $ eta$, $\eta$ and $
u$ of the three-dimensional $O(N)$ model in fixed dimension (massive zero-momentum scheme) were known to eighth order in the coupling. We extend them to tenth order, and $ eta$ to eleventh, for general $N$, which requires the two- and four-point functions to ten loops (1,593,254 graphs at the last order), and re-evaluate all lower orders. Through the Callan-Symanzik equation every coefficient follows from per-order sums that are linear in finite, zero-momentum $ ar R$-subtracted parametric integrals, one per graph, which we sample on GPUs by tropical Monte Carlo with densities adapted to the forest terms. The computation reproduces the known sums from two to seven loops within three standard deviations and agrees at ninth and tenth order, at lower precision, with an independent route through an intermediate scheme. The new coefficients have relative uncertainties of a few $10^{-5}$ or better, and the eighth-order coefficients of $\eta$ and $
u$ improve by factors of 120 and 4. The time needed to integrate an order to fixed relative precision grows by only 2.4-2.9 per loop from seven loops on, while the construction of the integrands still grows factorially and, at tenth order, costs more than the integration. Resummed, the tenth-order series give $
u=0.62997(51)$, $\eta=0.0333(18)$ and $\omega=0.803(14)$ for $N=1$, against $0.62997097(12)$, $0.036297612(48)$ and $0.82968(23)$ from the conformal bootstrap; at $N=3$ the deviations grow, so that the uncertainty is now dominated by the resummation rather than by the coefficients. Every result is generated automatically from, or checked against, a public ledger of independent, exactly pooled runs, hosted on GitHub, to which anyone is welcome to contribute computing time.

papers.title: Adiabatic Variational Principle: Born-Oppenheimer Theory for Emergent Electronic-Order Dynamics
papers.abstract: Recent advances in microscopic many-body methods have enabled increasingly accurate descriptions of equilibrium quantum states, yet large-scale simulations of emergent-order dynamics typically rely on phenomenological equations with prescribed free-energy functionals. We introduce the Adiabatic Variational Principle (AVP), a framework for deriving order-parameter dynamics directly from an interacting many-body Hamiltonian. When microscopic relaxation is fast compared with order-parameter evolution, the many-body state follows the collective configuration adiabatically, in analogy with the Born--Oppenheimer separation of electronic and nuclear motion. This assumption makes explicit the adiabatic closure implicit in conventional phase-field descriptions. Each instantaneous order-parameter configuration then defines a constrained quasi-stationary many-body state, and the Lagrange multipliers enforcing these constraints directly provide the thermodynamic forces driving the collective evolution. Nonlinear Mori--Zwanzig projection theory further connects the reversible dynamics to the microscopic algebra of the collective variables and relates dissipation and fluctuations to the eliminated degrees of freedom. Applications to charge- and spin-density-wave dynamics recover Allen--Cahn domain growth, resolve evolving domain networks together with their microscopic electronic structure, and yield generalized Landau--Lifshitz dynamics for itinerant magnetism. The AVP thus provides a solver-independent microscopic foundation for phase-field-like simulations of the nonequilibrium dynamics of emergent electronic order.

papers.title: Signature of Short-Range Order in Static Response of the Three-Dimensional Electron Gas
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional electron gas is a fundamental model in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, and the exchange-correlation energy derived from it serves as the starting point of \textit{ab initio} computations of materials. However, the wave-vector-dependent response, and hence the static local field factor $G(q)$, has remained without accurate ground-state benchmark in the strongly coupled regime for three decades. Using diffusion Monte Carlo, we calculate the static density-density response function and $G(q)$ across the liquid phase and find a pronounced structure in $G(q)$ at intermediate wave vectors, already visible at metallic densities and growing with increasing interaction strength. We identify it as a fingerprint of short-range order by showing that it is required to reproduce the static structure factor. Our parametrization, valid in the entire liquid phase, predicts a low-energy resonant mode inside the particle-hole continuum.

papers.title: Wave Turbulence of Capillary Waves in Finite Systems
papers.abstract: We consider classical problem of turbulence of capillary waves. In a series of numerical simulations it is shown that Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum corresponding to direct cascade of energy has a limited dynamic range of realization in a finite system, which shrinks with decreasing level of nonlinearity. Recent hypothesis that this dynamic range scales with average steepness as $\sim\mu^{8/3}$ is confirmed. As a byproduct the Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum was observed for record dynamic range close to or beyond one decade in a variety of simulation configurations.

papers.title: Inertial rotation of a small oblate spheroid in a simple shear flow
papers.abstract: We compare experiments and fully-resolved particle simulations designed to match the experimental conditions of a weakly inertial, neutrally buoyant, moderately oblate spheroid in shear flow under confinement. The study revisits an apparent discrepancy observed in earlier experiments, where a trajectory starting close to tumbling appeared to remain near the tumbling orbit, whereas weak-inertia theory predicts attraction to log-rolling for this particle shape. Experimental and numerical results are benchmarked against theory valid for asymptotically small particle Reynolds numbers and for unconfined systems. By accounting for confinement and inertia, together with sensitivity to initial conditions, and the finite observation time, we provide a consistent interpretation of the theoretical, experimental, and numerical results. Specifically, we show that log rolling is the only stable long-time orbit for the moderately oblate spheroid considered here; neither confinement nor finite inertia changes this orbit selection. Instead, inertia tends to accelerate the drift toward log rolling, whereas confinement reduces it, with the confinement effect being dominant in the present parameter range.

papers.title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization
papers.abstract: High-P\'eclet-number transport problems give rise to thin boundary layers with steep near-wall gradients whose accurate solution requires high-resolution meshes and could challenge inverse modeling. To address this challenge, we develop an overlapping Schwarz domain-decomposition framework grounded in perturbation theory, in which an inner equation governs near-wall dynamics and an outer equation governs bulk transport, and both subproblems are discretized using the finite element method and assembled into a fully differentiable multidomain physics solver. The formulation permits coarser mesh resolutions, reducing computational cost relative to a single-domain formulation. Exploiting the differentiability of the coupled solver, we formulate inverse problems in which the governing equations and boundary conditions are imposed as hard constraints, with the Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity. To accelerate the resulting adjoint-based optimization, we integrate large language models (LLMs) into the inverse workflow in two distinct configurations: a standalone optimizer that proposes successive parameter updates from the adjoint-computed sensitivities and an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) approach with access to the complete solver workflow, enabling it to perform multistage optimization procedures. The agentic AI configuration is shown to be most advantageous when the spatially varying unknown is represented in a functional basis rather than a high-dimensional nodal field representation. In this case, the AI agent grows the library of candidate basis functions during optimization under a prescribed admission policy, admitting predefined families in stages and initializing their parameters. In short, our proposed framework integrates Schwarz-coupled differentiable physics with agentic AI optimization for the inverse modeling of multiscale transport problems.

papers.title: Molecular Electrodynamic Relaxation in Dielectric and Plasmonic Cavities
papers.abstract: Molecular radiative emission is a fundamental relaxation process that governs excited-state lifetimes and significantly influences photophysical dynamics, but direct self-consistent Maxwell--Schr\"odinger simulations of molecular radiation suffer from numerical instabilities in evaluating radiative self-interaction. Herein, this issue is resolved within the self-consistent propagation of classical Maxwell's equations coupled to real-time density-functional electronic dynamics and their tight-binding approximation. By carefully removing the longitudinal components of radiative self-reaction, this framework quantitatively reproduces radiative lifetimes of atomic and molecular emitters in vacuum and further captures cavity-modified emission at weak and strong coupling regimes beyond perturbation theory. For molecules weakly coupled to an optical microcavity, the cavity Purcell effect is shown to reach maximum using a modestly red-detuned cavity due to nuclear thermal motion. Moreover, for a single methylene blue molecule strongly coupled to a realistic nanoparticle-on-mirror plasmonic cavity, the predicted molecular electrodynamical relaxation is accelerated to approximately 11 femtoseconds, directly competing with nonadiabatic nuclear dynamics. This work establishes a route to first-principles design of material radiative properties in a wide range of dielectric environments.

papers.title: Optimization of curved vortex generator geometry for enhanced thermal performance in water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger
papers.abstract: In the study, the geometry of curved rectangular vortex generators (RVG) has been optimized to enhance heat transfer and overall performance of the analyzed water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger (FTHE). The developed and validated conjugate numerical model includes a small section of the full-scale heat exchanger representing the computational domain, with fully developed velocity and temperature profiles specified at the inlet boundaries of the water. Four influential geometry parameters of the vortex generator were selected for the optimization; attack angle, curvature angle, axial position in the streamwise direction and height. The optimization process has been performed according to two criteria: maximization of heat transfer solely and maximization of heat transfer while considering the influence of pressure drop. Accordingly, one objective function related to the Colburn factor (j) and two objective functions combining the Colburn factor and the friction factor (f) were defined. The regression analysis has been used and the Central composite design of experiment was selected in order to obtain non-linear regression polynomial functions which were integrated into the investigated objectives. The optimization procedure has been performed using the genetic algorithm. Optimized configurations performance improvement was evaluated through comparison with the performance of the reference FTHE with plain fins. For the RVG configuration optimized according to the objective of maximizing heat transfer, the Colburn factor was enhanced by 53.1%. Optimizing the RVG configuration to maximize heat transfer while accounting for the influence of pressure drop resulted in an enhancement of the FTHE area goodness factor by 14.4% for one set of geometry parameters, and an enhancement of volume goodness factor by 26.5% for another.

papers.title: A Gaussian-Process Surrogate for Control Rod Worth with Calibrated Uncertainty: Application to VERA Core Physics Benchmark Problem 4
papers.abstract: Differential and integral control rod worth are usually obtained by differencing eigenvalue calculations at discrete rod positions, which resolves the derivative poorly and gives it no uncertainty. We build a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate for reactivity as a function of rod position on VERA Core Physics Benchmark Problem 4, a $3\times3$ assembly cluster with a hybrid AIC/B$_4$C rod cluster control assembly, modelled in OpenMC with ENDF/B-VIII.0. A parametric sigmoidal mean carries the dynamic range, a Matern-5/2 GP carries the residual, and the reported Monte Carlo uncertainty of each run enters as known observation noise. Because differentiation is linear, the differential rod worth and its variance follow in closed form from the kernel derivatives. Trained on 43 runs at three particle counts and tested on 11 independent runs, the surrogate meets a fixed 10 pcm accuracy target above the test-run noise, and its intervals are calibrated: the standardized leave-one-out residuals over 129 independent runs have variance 1.07 with 95% interval [0.85, 1.39]. The total worth agrees with the direct OpenMC end-point difference within combined uncertainty, and the differential worth peak is located to within one step. Three mean functions of very different fit quality give the same differential worth to within 0.1 pcm/step, while the width of its band depends on the kernel smoothness by a factor of four. The number of runs required and the remaining approximations are reported, and the extension to rod position and soluble boron is outlined.

papers.title: Predicting Weight Windows for Duct-Streaming Shielding Geometries with a Convolutional Neural Network
papers.abstract: Forward-flux-based weight windows give global variance reduction for duct-streaming shielding problems, but each new geometry needs an iterative Monte Carlo calculation to build them. We report preliminary results on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the map from a two-dimensional duct geometry and source position to the lower window bound of such an iteration, here the MAGIC generator in OpenMC, in milliseconds. A set of 250 random concrete ducts of three curved and rectangular families on the Protvino labyrinth bounding box was run in OpenMC with a Cf-252 point source and MAGIC generation, and a 1.9-million-parameter U-Net was trained on the logarithm of the lower bound. On held-out ducts the error in the cells that carry the flux is 0.14 to 0.51 decades; replicate MAGIC runs show this part of the map to be reproducible to a few hundredths of a decade, so the residual is model error, while below $10^{-6}$ the reference itself is noise. Applied without retraining to the rectangular Protvino labyrinth, the prediction correlates with MAGIC at 0.96. Used as weight windows there, with its deepest cells clamped at deployment, it gives an exit-detector figure of merit 54 times the analog value, 1.7 times that of the MAGIC generation run for the same geometry, and 0.80 of that of reused MAGIC windows whose construction it does not pay for. The run cost of any window set is shown to be set by its deepest cells and predictable from a population proxy.

papers.title: Generalizing Density Functional Theory with a Particle-Hole Expansion
papers.abstract: Strong electron correlation remains difficult to describe within conventional density functional approximations, particularly when natural-orbital occupations become strongly fractional. We introduce a systematic particle-hole expansion that generalizes density functional theory (DFT) through an explicit functional of the one-electron reduced density matrix. The previously derived cumulant-based correction emerges as the leading term and the thermal (entropic) correction as an infinite-order member whose coefficients are fixed by a single parameter. The expansion can be formulated as a moment problem solved by semidefinite programming with computational scaling comparable to DFT. We show that both the first- and second-order corrections yield closed-form natural-orbital occupations. Applications to periacenes and Fe-porphyrin demonstrate that the second-order correction substantially reduces excessive orbital fractionalization, yielding natural-orbital occupations and fundamental gaps in improved agreement with correlated calculations.
